title: How can we find our own pattern among the sequences?
description: One pattern is found among the sequences of the book. The gaps between neighbouring square numbers are looked at, and a picture of a growing square shows why they keep happening.
teaching_notes: One idea: find a pattern by looking at the gaps between neighbouring terms, test it on a few terms, then explain it with a picture. Watch for students who stop after one example and never ask why.

source: Figure it Out Q9 (Try This), p.9
video_script.why: The child learns how to hunt for a pattern: look at neighbouring terms, test on a few terms, and explain with a picture. One example shows the way, since this question has many answers.
video_script.substitution: This question is open ended, so the video shows one example, the gaps between neighbouring square numbers.
video_script.anchor: a square of dots that grows by an L shaped border of dots
video_script.payoff_line: The gaps between neighbouring squares are the odd numbers, from an L shaped border of dots

final_answer.value: one example: the gaps between neighbouring squares 3, 5, 7, 9, ... are the odd numbers (open ended)
final_answer.spoken: the gaps are the odd numbers

maths_rules: a 3 by 3 square of 9 dots becomes a 4 by 4 square of 16 dots by adding an L shaped border of 7 dots: a row of 4 and a column of 3
check: 5 by 5 from 4 by 4 adds a row of 5 and a column of 4, 9 dots, and 16 + 9 = 25
the question is open ended; any pattern that is tested and explained is acceptable
video_script.design: The squares are drawn as grids of dots. The gaps between neighbours are written. One grid grows into the next by an L shaped border.
open_questions: The book question is open ended with no single answer; one example pattern is shown.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about finding your own pattern.
<bookmark mark='seq'/>You can pick any of the sequences. Here we pick the squares, one, four, nine, sixteen and twenty five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What pattern can we find in them, and why does it happen?

beats.on_screen: the squares stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the squares drawn as grids of dots: 1, 4, 9, 16; a gap arrow between each neighbouring pair

marks.way: the squares move to the side
marks.dots: each square is drawn as a square grid of dots
marks.gap: a gap arrow joins each pair of neighbours

beats.colours: dots in blue, gap arrows in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='dots'/>Each square is a square grid of dots.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>A gap is how much more one number is than the one before it.

marks.given: the squares are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the squares one, four, nine, sixteen and twenty five.

beats.on_screen: To find: a pattern in the gaps between neighbouring squares, and why it happens
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find a pattern in the gaps between neighbouring squares, and explain it.

marks.first: the first two gaps are written
marks.second: the last two gaps are written

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, find the gap between each pair of neighbours. Four minus one is three, and nine minus four is five.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Sixteen minus nine is seven, and twenty five minus sixteen is nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: test the idea: the gaps 3, 5, 7, 9 each go up by 2

marks.look: the four gaps are lined up with arrows between them

narration: <bookmark mark='look'/>Step two, look at the gaps three, five, seven and nine.
<bookmark mark='plus'/>Each gap is two more than the one before it. We can test this idea on more squares too.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: picture: a 3 by 3 square of 9 dots grows into a 4 by 4 square of 16 dots by an L shaped border of 7 dots

marks.three: a square of three rows of three dots appears
marks.border: a row of four dots and a column of three dots are added as an L shaped border
marks.count: the border dots are counted as seven

beats.colours: old square in blue, new border in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step three, draw a square of three rows of three dots.
<bookmark mark='border'/>To make the next square, add a row of four dots and a column of three dots.
<bookmark mark='count'/>That L shaped border has seven dots, which is the gap between nine and sixteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: 4 by 4 grows into 5 by 5 with a row of 5 and a column of 4 = 9 dots, and 16 + 9 = 25

marks.check: a row of five dots and a column of four dots are added to the four by four square, giving nine more dots and twenty five in all

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check the next square. A row of five dots and a column of four dots make nine. Sixteen plus nine is twenty five.

beats.on_screen: Answer: one pattern: the gaps 3, 5, 7, 9, ... are the odd numbers; each new square adds an L shaped border of dots

marks.ans: the gaps are boxed with their name beside the L shaped border

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The gaps between neighbouring squares are the odd numbers, from an L shaped border of dots. You can find other patterns the same way.
